title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?

source_formulation.text: The computational complexity of the 3-Edge Colorability-problem for planar graphs remains open, while it is known to be NP-complete already for 3-regular, but not necessarily […]

why: This is a basic unresolved coloring decision problem on planar graphs with very small maximum degree. A resolution would clarify exactly how far the algorithmic consequences of the Four-Color Theorem extend beyond regular planar graphs.
status_note: The question is open in the 2022 source and explicitly retained in the journal version published online on 25 November 2025. These source statements were checked on 13 September 2026; no subsequent resolution was verified. Status is source_open.

progress.text: The source gives polynomial-time recognition of graphs admitting a cubic bridgeless planar augmentation while explicitly leaving general planar three-edge-colorability open.
The expanded journal version retains the general coloring question and distinguishes it from its polynomial and hardness results for specified supergraph recognition tasks.

category_assignment.reason: The problem is the algorithmic classification of edge coloring on planar graphs.

importance.reason: A fundamental unresolved planar edge-coloring decision problem at maximum degree three, closely tied to the boundary of Four-Color-Theorem consequences.

sentences: Three-edge-colorability asks whether the edges of a graph can receive three colors with different colors on every pair meeting at a vertex.
The selected question asks for the computational complexity of this decision problem on planar graphs.
The source studies a sufficient route through augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph, where three-edge-colorability follows from the Four-Color Theorem.
It also discusses a conjectured characterization for two-connected planar graphs of maximum degree three.
A full classification would determine whether the remaining planar cases admit an efficient coloring test or conceal an NP-hard obstruction.

definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.

context_blocks.text: The source poses this as Question 1 and explains why the Four-Color Theorem settles the cubic bridgeless case without settling all subcubic planar graphs. A graph with degree-two vertices need not lie in a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph.

The 2022 paper gives a polynomial-time test for augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph. Its concluding discussion keeps general planar three-edge-colorability open and states a stronger proposed structural characterization.

The expanded journal article, published online in November 2025 and appearing in Algorithmica’s 2026 volume, again poses planar three-edge-colorability as an open question. Its recognition results concern specified cubic supergraphs and do not identify that augmentation task with the full coloring decision problem.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.
